text:
[LNUL.4.8] **A GUARD admits on `null`, and that is the opposite of
[LNUL.4.3].** A guard is an engine-evaluated expression that decides whether an
**already-matched** activation is withheld — the compiler-emitted cooldown gate
is the one v1 has ([IRET.25.5.1]). Where the guard evaluates to `null`, the
runtime **must** let the activation proceed. Only an explicit `false` suppresses.

A time-dependent condition that the runtime reads beside the gate is not a guard
([RDSC.4a.8.2.2]): it decides whether the rule matches, and [LNUL.4.3] governs it.

The value is still `null` and Kleene still holds ([LNUL.4.2]); what this clause
settles is the **disposition of `null` at this site**, which [LNUL.4.3] settles
the other way at its own.

**Why the two differ, because a single default cannot serve both.** A `where`
clause decides whether a rule *matches*: declining to fire on an unknown is
cautious, recoverable, and visible in the next cycle when the value arrives —
*don't act on what you don't know*. A guard decides whether a rule that has
already matched is *held back*. Suppressing on an unknown does not decline to
act; it **deletes the rule for as long as the value is absent**, and nothing
distinguishes that from a rule whose conditions are simply never met.

So the safe direction inverts with the site. A guard that cannot establish
grounds for suppression has not established them, and the activation stands.
Firing more often than the author intended is bounded and observable; a rule
that silently ceases to exist is neither.

⚠ **No test can distinguish the two policies**, which is why this needs stating
rather than discovering. The two agree on every value that evaluates, so a suite
over evaluable data returns identical results under either. Only an
unevaluable guard separates them, and a fixture has to be written to produce one.
